prompt: Why does `ORDER BY placed_at DESC LIMIT 5` need no Sort node when `placed_at` has a B-tree?
hint: What order are the index entries in?

choices.text: The index is read backwards from its end
choices.why: Right: the entries are already sorted, and the Limit stops after five.

choices.text: PostgreSQL caches the last five rows of every table in memory for this
choices.why: There is no such cache; the plan is an Index Scan Backward.

choices.text: The table itself is stored in placed_at order, so no index is used
choices.why: The plan names orders_placed_at_idx; a table has no guaranteed order.

choices.text: A Sort node is there but hidden by EXPLAIN when LIMIT is small
choices.why: EXPLAIN hides no nodes; the plan is Limit over Index Scan Backward.

prompt: `customers.email` has a unique B-tree, and `LIKE 'user42@%'` still gets a sequential scan. Why?
hint: Look at how text is sorted in that database.

choices.text: Unique indexes are never used for LIKE
choices.why: Uniqueness has nothing to do with it; a non-unique index on the same collation fails the same way.

choices.text: The pattern has an @, which LIKE treats as a wildcard
choices.why: Only % and _ are wildcards in LIKE.

choices.text: The index uses the column's collation, and PostgreSQL 16 only turns a prefix into a range under C
choices.why: Right: C.UTF-8 does not count, so the planner needs text_pattern_ops.

choices.text: customers is too small for an index to be worth it
choices.why: With text_pattern_ops the same query used an index at cost 8.44.

prompt: Which of these can a `text_pattern_ops` index on `email` serve?
hint: A prefix is a range; a suffix is not.

choices.text: `email LIKE '%@example.com'`
choices.why: A leading wildcard is not a range in any order; it stayed a sequential scan.

choices.text: `email LIKE 'user7%'`
choices.why: Right: a prefix becomes the range from user7 to user8.

choices.text: `ORDER BY email` in the database's collation
choices.why: Its order is byte order, not the collation's; the ordinary index serves that.

choices.text: `lower(email) = 'user7@example.com'`
choices.why: A function of the column needs an index on that expression, lesson 9's subject.

prompt: What can a hash index answer?
hint: It keeps hash codes, not an order.

choices.text: Equality, ranges and ORDER BY, faster than a B-tree
choices.why: Without an order it answers no range and no ORDER BY.

choices.text: Equality and prefix searches
choices.why: A prefix is a range, which needs order.

choices.text: Only =
choices.why: Right: the email > query went to the B-tree instead.

choices.text: Equality, and uniqueness when declared UNIQUE
choices.why: A hash index cannot enforce UNIQUE; only a B-tree can.

prompt: The B-tree on `customers.email` was 14 MB and the hash index on the same column 6568 kB. Roughly what fraction of the B-tree's size is the hash, as a percentage?
hint: 6568 kB is about 6.4 MB.

prompt: Why would a hash index on `customers.email` not let you drop the B-tree there?
hint: What does the B-tree do besides speed up lookups?

choices.text: Because two indexes on one column always perform better than one
choices.why: Each extra index costs every write; more is not better by itself.

choices.text: Because the B-tree enforces the UNIQUE constraint
choices.why: Right: a hash index cannot enforce it, so the B-tree stays whatever else exists.

choices.text: Because hash indexes are not crash-safe
choices.why: That stopped being true in PostgreSQL 10.

choices.text: Because the hash index is only used after the B-tree is warm
choices.why: The planner chose the hash index for equality with the B-tree present.

prompt: What does a GIN index on `tags` keep?
hint: Inverted.

choices.text: Each array, sorted as a whole value
choices.why: That is a B-tree over arrays, which cannot find one element.

choices.text: For each tag, the rows that contain it
choices.why: Right: eleven entries, one per tag, each with its list of products.

choices.text: A hash of each array
choices.why: A hash of the whole array answers only whether two arrays are equal.

choices.text: The smallest and largest tag of every 128 pages
choices.why: That is BRIN's summary, and it would not find tags inside arrays.

prompt: The GIN index took the tag search from 58.7 ms to 19.8 ms under load. Where did most of the remaining time go?
hint: A fifth of all products wear the tag.

choices.text: Into the Bitmap Index Scan on the GIN index
choices.why: That took about 1.4 ms of the 17.

choices.text: Into planning, since GIN plans are expensive to make
choices.why: Planning Time was 0.63 ms.

choices.text: Into the network round trip to pgbench
choices.why: pgbench ran on the same machine; EXPLAIN ANALYZE showed 17 ms inside the server.

choices.text: Into reading all 649 pages and sorting 9917 rows
choices.why: Right: the WHERE was answered, and the ORDER BY LIMIT was the costly half.

prompt: With a B-tree on `price_cents`, the tag search read 74 rows instead of 9917. Why so few?
hint: The index hands rows over in price order.

choices.text: The B-tree also indexes the tags
choices.why: It indexes only price_cents; the tag test is a Filter, with 54 rows removed.

choices.text: Walking from the cheapest, one in five carries the tag, so twenty turn up quickly and the Limit stops
choices.why: Right: about a hundred rows were expected and 74 were read.

choices.text: The planner switched to a sample of the table
choices.why: Plans never sample; the answer is exact.

choices.text: The GIN index pre-filtered the rows
choices.why: The plan used only products_price_cents_idx.

prompt: A search for the tag `kitchn`, which no product has, took 41 ms with both indexes present. What made the planner pick the slow plan?
hint: Compare rows= with what came out.

choices.text: The GIN index was not valid yet
choices.why: It had been used for kitchen minutes earlier.

choices.text: GIN cannot answer a search that matches nothing
choices.why: An empty list is the cheapest answer GIN gives.

choices.text: It expected 250 rows, so the walk looked short
choices.why: Right: with no match the walk read all 50,000 products. A wrong estimate picked between two good indexes.

choices.text: B-trees take priority over GIN when both apply
choices.why: There is no priority; the planner compares estimated costs.

prompt: Which statements about `jsonb_path_ops` compared with the default `jsonb_ops` match this lesson? Choose all that apply.
hint: Sizes, build times and operators.

choices.text: It was smaller, 42 MB against 55 MB
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It built faster, 9.6 s against 20.8 s
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It answers the ? operator, does this key exist
choices.why: Only jsonb_ops does; jsonb_path_ops answers @> only.

choices.text: The planner chose it for @> when both existed
choices.why: Right: the plan named events_payload_path_idx.

prompt: What does a GiST trigram index offer that a GIN trigram index does not?
hint: Look at the Order By line in the plan.

choices.text: Support for ILIKE with a leading wildcard
choices.why: Both serve that, and GIN is usually faster for it.

choices.text: Nearest-first ordering by distance
choices.why: Right: the index itself hands rows over by <-> distance and the Limit stops.

choices.text: Case-insensitive equality on titles
choices.why: That is an expression index on lower(title).

choices.text: A smaller index than the table
choices.why: Both are smaller than the table; that is not what sets GiST apart.

prompt: A booking table must refuse two bookings of the same room that overlap in time. Which tool does the lesson point to?
hint: Two overlapping ranges are not equal.

choices.text: A UNIQUE constraint on (room, during)
choices.why: Two different ranges that overlap are not equal, so UNIQUE lets both in.

choices.text: A SELECT for overlaps before every INSERT
choices.why: Two requests arriving together both find nothing and both insert.

choices.text: A BRIN index on the start time
choices.why: BRIN speeds up range reads; it enforces nothing.

choices.text: EXCLUDE USING gist (room WITH =, during WITH &&), with btree_gist
choices.why: Right: the shape of seller_away, with btree_gist for the = on an ordinary type.

prompt: The extension that cuts strings into runs of three characters, so that `ILIKE '%…%'` can use an index, is ___.
hint: Its name ends in trgm.

prompt: What does a BRIN index store for each range of 128 pages?
hint: One small summary per stretch.

choices.text: Every value in the range, sorted
choices.why: That would be as big as a B-tree; BRIN was 32 kB.

choices.text: A pointer to each row whose value changed
choices.why: BRIN keeps no per-row pointers at all.

choices.text: The smallest and largest value
choices.why: Right: and a search skips every range they rule out.

choices.text: The number of rows in the range and their average
choices.why: An average cannot rule a value out; BRIN keeps the minimum and maximum.

prompt: A BRIN index on `events.customer_id` made `customer_id = 4242` take 445 ms. Which number would have warned you before you built it?
hint: Lesson 7 read it for every column.

choices.text: n_distinct of customer_id, 181538
choices.why: Many distinct values do not hurt BRIN if they are in table order.

choices.text: correlation, -0.0032
choices.why: Right: no relation to table order, so every range covers every customer.

choices.text: null_frac, 0.3054
choices.why: NULLs are recorded separately in BRIN's summary and are not the problem.

choices.text: The size of the table, 511 MB
choices.why: The same table gave 18 ms for a day of at.

prompt: A day's events by `at` with the BRIN index showed `Heap Blocks: lossy=896`. With 128 pages per range, how many ranges is that?
hint: Divide.

prompt: Match each question to the index type this lesson used for it.
hint: One structure per shape of question.

pairs.left: events whose payload contains a product
a day of events in a table written in time order

prompt: Order the indexes on `events.at` and `customers.email` measured in this lesson from smallest to largest.
items: B-tree of the UNIQUE on customers.email
trap: A B-tree on five million timestamps is the largest by far.

prompt: A table of sensor readings is append-only and queried by time ranges, and its B-tree on `read_at` is now a fifth of the disk. What does the lesson suggest checking first?
hint: BRIN makes a bet.

choices.text: Whether a hash index on read_at would be smaller
choices.why: A hash index cannot answer ranges at all.

choices.text: Whether its correlation is near 1, for BRIN
choices.why: Right: a time column in a table that only grows at the end follows table order, and then BRIN is a few kB.

choices.text: Whether GIN supports timestamps
choices.why: GIN is for values made of parts; a timestamp has none.

choices.text: Whether the B-tree needs a REINDEX
choices.why: A rebuilt B-tree on every row would still be far larger than a BRIN.

prompt: A screen lists the ten newest orders with a given status, `WHERE status = $1 ORDER BY placed_at DESC LIMIT 10`, and is slow. Applying this lesson's tag-search finding, which index is worth trying first?
hint: The question is the whole text, not its WHERE.

choices.text: A hash index on status
choices.why: It finds the rows but hands them over in no order, so the sort remains.

choices.text: A GIN index on status
choices.why: status is a single word, not a value made of parts.

choices.text: A two-column B-tree, filter column first
choices.why: Right: it finds one status and walks it already in placed_at order, so the Limit stops at ten.

choices.text: A BRIN index on status
choices.why: status does not follow table order, so every range would match.
